claims.text: The starting nanoparticles are homogeneous, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
The starting nanoparticles have high surface area and no pre-formed oxide layer.
Low, controlled oxygen exposure at high temperature produces mild surface oxidation of the nanoparticles.
Mild controlled oxidation forms a thin, passivating oxide layer on the nanoparticle surfaces.
The passivating oxide layer may be enriched in Cr or other readily oxidizable alloy constituents.
A passivating surface oxide retards surface diffusion.
Retarding surface diffusion suppresses elemental segregation.
Suppressing elemental segregation prevents phase decomposition and helps preserve the solid-solution structure at high temperature.
Without surface passivation, elemental rearrangement and phase decomposition are accelerated.
Long-term high-temperature annealing can decompose initially solid-solution high-entropy alloys into multiphase microstructures.
Nanoparticles treated at low oxygen partial pressure will exhibit less segregation and phase decomposition than nanoparticles treated in an oxygen-free inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticles annealed in an inert atmosphere will show relatively pronounced elemental segregation and phase decomposition over time.
Oxidative stabilization requires constituents capable of forming a sufficiently protective oxide layer.
Excessive oxygen may produce thick, non-protective oxide scales that promote degradation.
Systems lacking sufficiently oxidizable constituents will not form an adequate passivation layer.
The oxide-layer thickness, composition, and protective effectiveness may vary because nanoparticle behavior differs from bulk behavior.
The stabilization mechanism may differ across the 473–1923 K thermoelectric range and the 773–1173 K catalytic range.
